name: Nonapeptide-1
lead: Nonapeptide-1, sold under the trade name Melanostatine, is a short synthetic peptide of nine amino acids used in skin-brightening and dark-spot products. It is described as a melanocortin antagonist: it is designed to compete with alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH) at the MC1 receptor on pigment cells, which is one of the signals that tells skin to make melanin.[2][3]

People use it in serums and creams aimed at a more even, brighter complexion, including fading the look of sun spots and melasma-type patches. It is usually found alongside other brightening ingredients rather than on its own.[1]

Published human research is small. A randomized pilot study in 46 people with melasma tested a combination product containing phenyl ethyl resorcinol, nonapeptide-1, aminoethyl phosphinic acid and antioxidants plus sunscreen against sunscreen alone as a maintenance regimen.[1] Laboratory studies have also used nonapeptide-1 as a reference or building block in pigment research.[2][3]

chain: Blocks alpha-MSH signalling at the MC1 receptor
angle.text: Nonapeptide-1 is applied topically in brightening serums to reduce the pigment signals behind dark spots and uneven tone. People use it as part of a routine aimed at a clearer, more uniform complexion.

infobox: Skin brightening, dark spots, melasma-type pigmentation

paras: Nonapeptide-1 is formulated into topical brightening serums, creams and spot treatments. The goal is a more even skin tone and a reduction in the appearance of hyperpigmented patches, such as sun-induced spots and melasma.[1]
It appears in multi-ingredient formulas, for example alongside phenyl ethyl resorcinol, aminoethyl phosphinic acid, antioxidants and sunscreen in a product studied for melasma maintenance.[1]

UV exposure prompts skin cells to release alpha-MSH, which binds the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) on melanocytes and drives melanin production. Researchers note that alpha-MSH antagonists could therefore have applications in preventing melanogenesis.[2]
Nonapeptide-1 is described as interfering with this signalling, and a 2024 paper describes it as having melanin-transfer-interfering properties that reduce melanin content in treated skin areas.[3]

A prospective, double-blinded, parallel-group randomized pilot study enrolled 46 people with melasma, 23 in each arm, over eight months. It compared a proprietary combination containing nonapeptide-1 with sunscreen alone as maintenance after initial triple-combination treatment, and also assessed safety and quality of life.[1] Because the product contained several active ingredients, the study examined the combination rather than nonapeptide-1 alone.

In cell studies, human keratinocytes and epidermal melanocytes exposed to UVA were treated with tea polyphenols or nonapeptide-1 acetate salt as part of an investigation of the alpha-MSH-MC1R pathway.[2] A 2024 study loaded green-tea EGCG onto nonapeptide-1-conjugated silica nanoparticles and reported reduced melanin and DNA damage in skin cells exposed to UV.[3]

card.summary: A nine-amino-acid peptide (Melanostatine) used in serums to dial down pigment signals for a brighter, more even skin tone.

quick.overview:
Nonapeptide-1 is a small cosmetic peptide used in skin-brightening products. People use it to help fade the look of dark spots and even out skin tone.

It is typically one ingredient among several in a brightening serum or melasma-maintenance product, often paired with sunscreen.
quick.mechanism: It is described as a melanocortin antagonist: it competes with alpha-MSH at the MC1 receptor on melanocytes, which reduces the signal to produce melanin, and it is reported to interfere with melanin transfer.
quick.risks: It is applied topically and sold as a cosmetic ingredient. Published human data are limited to a small pilot trial of a multi-ingredient product, so its individual effects have not been separately studied in people.
